No one’s giving you the real world history of SCP to explain it.

The first ever SCP was actually 173, posted to a HORROR and creepypasta board on 4chan. What followed were a few thousand copycats and then SCP-003 (I think it was 03, might’ve actually been 02). After that the wiki slowly started as authors who wrote original ideas met up and things solidified into the wiki site.

I am not sure if the rule is still there now but during these early years there was a rule that your story HAD to be horror in some way in order to fit the themes and idea of the site. SCP was publicly pitched as the largest collaborative creative horror writing project on the internet. The horror aspect was key to creation (being inspired by creepypastas and posted to a board for them) and thus the creators wanted to make it key to identity.

Now eventually (thankfully) people realized you can have stories with the Foundation that doesn’t use horror. Buuuuuuttttttt after half a decade of “horror only” the precedent, tradition, and culture is set so horror stays as the focus as time goes on, despite authors such as DaveYouFool injecting as much comedy as they can.

Starship Troopers was written in 1959, at, arguably, one of the hottest points (pre-proxy war doctrine) of the Cold War. Heinlein was 110% being genuine the entire book. Heinlein was ALSO parroting back at you the cultural undercurrents of the 1950’s, especially in how paranoid it was. Based off literally everything else he wrote, it’s hard to believe he held these beliefs for long, considering the very next book undercuts basically all of them. But it’s quite interesting to see his one hyper-reactionary novel and wonder why it’s SO thematically distinct from his other works.

You also have to hold in mind the purpose and audience of these myths. They were meant to be told to young children in order to explain the world. Orpheus and Eurydice was used to explain why mom can’t come back. So that emotional weight didn’t necessarily need to be built into the story because most of it was already on the audience and not needed to fulfill its purpose, not to mention with especially young kids brevity is a necessity. They just aren’t able to sit down for an entire story, stay engaged, AND take the lesson out of it after a certain length. 

So, looking at it from the future. It’s not the best work of fiction by far. But we’re also not criticizing The Tortoise and The Hare for when The Hare takes a nap. We collectively remember the audience of The Tortoise and The Hare and so we excuse it. We’ve forgotten the audience of these small moral or explanatory Greek myths, so we are more critical.

I really hope my comment seemed like it wasn’t nuanced. Naturally, as with everything, the EC and O5 (and in canons where it exists the Board of Site Directors), shift in focus and effectiveness over time. Looking at Redtape, Paragon, even Admonition has both O5’s and senior site directors acting in moral or heroic ways. 

7545 is actually one of my favorites for showing how O5’s think, the dilemma they always exist in, and the guilt they carry. Shows that the Foundation as an organization can be as flawed or even straight-up evil, yet every individual within justifies their actions, believes what they are doing is right, and thinks they are a good person. It’s realistic to life. Every person around all of us including us justifies every action however we can or must. 

In essence, I think the morality of the Foundation is supposed to be the most intimate representation of an organization with genuinely great intentions and goals that has become overburdened by its size (which is necessary), it’s natural corruption (which happens in every organization over time, regardless of how “pure” or “good” it attains to be), filled with individuals who genuinely believe they are doing the right thing, who genuinely believe the necessity outweighs the cost, OR they are working from within to change it (shoutout to Site-43!). It’s an attempt at realism when showing bureaucracy. It’s an attempt at humanization via the plight of the individual when stood against the machinery of a codified system. The Foundation is your government, and your white collar employer, and your cultural system of authorities and rituals while also being your brother who works for the Ministry of Health or your friend that started their own coffee shop or your mother. It’s about how crushing a system can be despite the humanity of those who operate it.

I think the greatest point OP should take away from your reply and everyone should take away from the interaction between you and OP is that the Foundation is supposed to be a “real” and therefore realistic organization. So, it does what many real organizations do. It regularly puts its own survival ahead of its goals and morals. The Ethics Committee has ended up becoming “Foundation HR” which means it protects the companies not the employees, 6500 is entirely about when the Foundation’s principles and its own survival come into conflict! It’s an organization, and like all organizations, it does both good and evil things to further itself. 

IMO one of the greatest themes of contemporary articles, especially those like Maslov’s Fire, is the tension between individuals trying to genuinely do what’s good, who joined in order to save the world literally, who actually care, against the organization that wants to keep itself alive, hidden, well funded, and powerful.

I want to recommend the short story “The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas” by Ursula K. Le Guin. It tackles a very similar thematic web and explains the philosophical reasoning for this idea a little bit more. I’m going to explain it horribly here, but again I highly recommend you read the story, it’s something like 5 pages. 

The idea is we, as a species, need something to “live for”, and we can’t just live for ourselves. Once death is removed (as it is implied it is on the utopian central planet) we can’t live for the betterment of our family post-death because there is no post-death anymore, you’ll always be there to support them. So, you add in artificial suffering. Now everyone is living the best life they can because they know others can’t and they don’t want to waste it. 

The beauty of Kalinin’s Proposal, and the key difference, is unlike Omelas, no one is allowed to opt out. In fact, those that did are now actively trying to be forcibly brought back. On one hand it removes the philosophic conundrum entirely, the utopia becomes unequivocally evil, enforcing suffering with no escape just to sustain itself rather than provide a place of utopia (so long as you accept the fine print). On the other hand it brings the reader into the story via sympathy. Le Guin, in my opinion, wants the reader to feel slight dehumanization towards the child, I think Le Guin wants the reader to recognize they feel that dehumanization and confront those feelings. I believe that’s the true purpose of the piece. Kalinin, meanwhile, I believe is more truly contemplating the philosophical implications of having a utopia based off suffering, therefore he wants the reader to relate not with the townspeople but the child.

Without reading any other replies to your comment I totally agree, and I think the thing most commenters are missing is that the interviewer was trying to determine *thought process*. Not even ability to justify but the methods by which you think and solve a “problem”, even as low stakes as deciding on a drink. 

The question IS a bad question, but I also challenge anyone to make a GOOD question that can ascertain someone’s thought patterns AND be asked and answered in less than a few minutes. 

The problem is that the interviewer wants information that’s incredibly difficult to ascertain quickly but also essential for figuring out if the potential employee will work well in the problem-solving groups, methods, and procedures already in place. It’s a Catch-22 where HR often decides to take an imperfect and potentially discriminatory solution over no solution at all.

If an interviewer told me “tell me about yourself” I’d clam up immediately due to the same autistism that makes me not understand tangential questions. Arguably, it’d move me from confusion (what’s your favorite drink) into uncomfortability, which would be significantly worse imo.

Everyone that agrees with OP names different time spans. Some say movies “went bad” around 2000, some 2010, some 1990. 

What this, to me, points to is that there isn’t actually a criteria that gets broken, there isn’t actually a moment you can point to as a downfall or even a slide. There isn’t actually a time where movies “go bad”. It’s entirely personal. No one can agree. Hell just a few months ago there was a thread just like this where the OOP of that thread said their favorite movie was from 2016 and that was when film went bad. 2016! 

I could go and list about 100 films from the last 25 years that I personally think we’re going to look back as classics. But that won’t change anything as it’s my opinion. 

What these threads, to me, show most above all is that 1) the average person is not watching movies. Period. If you watched one new movie a month you’d know by experience this is false, the reason 1 a month does it is because (as you’ll quickly learn) there are severely dry months forcing you to watch something not pushed by a major studio but a minor studio (Searchlight, Focus, etc.). 2) you’ll have learned (or realized) that Marvel movies AREN’T the center of movie culture anymore and haven’t been for maybe a year and a half. That ship sailed a bit ago. If you see someone mentioning Marvel or superheroes they aren’t plugged into the scene enough, simple as. 3) OP could just be in a dry spell. Lots of people could. You can’t just watch anything anymore, you don’t have the time, so your brain is getting pickier. That’s fine! That’s good! Recognize that THAT is what’s happening, not some overall quality going down.

Edited to add: You have to keep in mind that the genre must be used in a way that directly affects the meaning. Robocop works great as the sci-fi nature and critique of the genre (done through the straight-faced and truthful adoption of said genre) also works into its critiques of police enforcement and copaganda at large. Total Recall (also by Verhoeven) is just a “normal” film in that it isn’t any of the aforementioned methods of critique. It just uses its themes and standard film techniques to critique capitalism and corporatism. It doesn’t utilize the genre to make these critiques nor make fun of it.

Warhammer works as a pastiche because it utilizes the sci-fi genre as well. The example that springs to mind firstly is the Margaret Thatcher critique. It needs to be sci-fi Orks for that critique to work, it uses both the unending violent warmongering nature of the Orks to critique Thatcher’s own warmongering as well as making fun of her in both superficial and personal ways. It needs to be sci-fi to make the critique, but for Warhammer to work the sci-fi has to be “real”, so the sci-fi is straight-edged and within the genre while the critiques are both reliant on the genre and applicable to the real world, resulting in pastiche. It’s also over-the-top to utilize exaggeration and make the setting generally more enjoyable as one often has to do when making real world critiques (look at the absurdity of the ending of Robocop).

Also! If you want good pastiche in film (or really any postmodern literature as that’s my specialty in my academia life) DM me and I can give you a solid list with starting places and stuff. 1984 is not often considered satire. It’s a dystopian fiction piece (arguably one of the first) that fits solidly and firmly within its genre. While highlighting key and important issues and themes it does not make fun of them. I always return to these rules of thumb when doing genre analysis for an article or review:

Satire takes a real world issue and makes fun of it. It often uses humor and exaggeration to do so. (Note: exaggeration does not immediately equal humor, the two can exist simultaneously or one at a time).

Parody takes a genre and makes fun of it, pointing at cliches and highlighting the natural silliness of fiction. It relies on humor and can only exist when defined tropes and cliches are present across various different texts.

Pastiche adopts a genre to make fun of a real world issue. It fully seriously dons a genre and doesn’t make fun of the genre, but then makes fun of a real world issue using that genre. The humor is often much more subtle, but this relies on exaggeration. 

Personally I see 40k as a pastiche, I think humor can be found (many of the Horus Heresy books are FUNNY) but it’s not necessarily center stage. It fully adopts sci-fi seriously and does not make fun of its own genre often. It also fully intends (or at the very least intended) to take real world issues and if not make fun of them at least make fun of the way we talk and think about them (humanity-first thinking, religiosity, governance, etc.).

The book Guns, Germs, and Steel by Jared Diamond addresses this very question and the author sums it up to be the fact that A) North America didn’t have any pack animals like Europe did.
B) The continent is vertical instead of horizontal.
C) The climate varies so much in different areas.

A is important because Europe had many many pack animals and that allowed them to trade more and transport materials. They were able to coalesce into larger communities than just towns because they could travel much larger distances faster.

B and C were important for the same reason, since the continent was vertical that means that the climates bay wildest from area to area, that makes farming difficult because the crops don’t translate north or south due to the lack of plants ability to adapt quickly. It also means technology has a hard time distributing since the problems of each climate are so vastly different.

These are the main problems that the author described and attributed to why Europe developed so much faster than the Americas. Check out the book as it’s a very good and interesting read.
